title: Rotate Array
directAnswer: Rotate the array right by k steps in-place. First reduce k with k %= n (k can exceed n). The O(1)-space trick is three reversals: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k elements, then reverse the remaining n−k. That lands every element in its rotated position without an auxiliary array. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.formula:
k %= n
reverse(nums, 0, n - 1)
reverse(nums, 0, k - 1)
reverse(nums, k, n - 1)
rules: **Always `k %= n` first** — k can be larger than n, and rotating by n is a no-op.
Right-rotate by k means the **last k elements move to the front**, in their original order.
Three reversals: **whole → first k → last n−k**. Doing first-k before the whole reversal rotates the wrong way.
The reversal swaps are a two-pointer walk from both ends toward the middle — O(1) space.
The extra-array method is O(n) space but the clearest correctness proof: `out[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]`.
whenToUse: Cyclically shift an array/string in-place with O(1) extra space
Any 'rotate by k' where k may exceed the length
When the interviewer bans an auxiliary array
antiSignals: You may use O(n) extra space and want the simplest code → index-mapping copy
Rotation is conceptual only (just need element at rotated index) → compute (i - k) % n on read, don't move data
Linked list rotation → relink pointers, not reversals (LC 61)
2D matrix rotation → transpose + reflect, a different mechanic (LC 48)
remember.takeaway: Three reversals turn an O(n)-space rotation into O(1) space. The identity 'reverse all, then reverse each block' is the reusable insight — it also rotates strings and underlies the classic 'rotate words in a sentence' problem.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you remember k %= n, and whether you know the three-reversal O(1)-space rotation rather than only the easy extra-array copy.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting k %= n (TLE or out-of-bounds when k > n), or rotating one element at a time k times, which is O(n·k).
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Start with the O(n)-space index map to prove correctness, then deliver the three-reversal O(1) method and explain WHY the reversals compose into a rotation.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums`, rotate the array to the right by `k` steps, where `k` is non-negative.

Do it **in-place** with `O(1)` extra space if you can — that's the follow-up the interviewer cares about.
understanding: Shift every element k positions to the right, wrapping the last k elements around to the front. Element originally at index i ends at index (i + k) % n. Because k may exceed n, reduce it modulo n before doing any work.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can k be larger than the array length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — k ≤ 10⁵ regardless of n. Rotating by n returns the original, so the effective rotation is k %= n. Skipping this causes out-of-bounds or wasted work.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Right rotation or left?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Right. The last k elements wrap to the front. A left rotation by k is equivalent to a right rotation by n − k, so the same machinery applies.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is O(1) extra space required?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's the follow-up that distinguishes answers. The extra-array copy is accepted, but the three-reversal method is what they're probing for.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array contain duplicates or negatives?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, both. Rotation only moves positions, so values are irrelevant to correctness.

examples.explanation: The last 3 elements (5,6,7) wrap to the front; the first 4 shift right by 3.
Last 2 elements (3,99) move to the front.
k %= n → 3 % 2 = 1, so a single right rotation.

approaches.name: Extra Array via Index Mapping (Brute / Correctness Proof)
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first — it's the cleanest proof of WHERE each element goes. Then pivot to the O(1)-space follow-up.
hints: Where does the element at index i end up after a right rotation by k? Write the destination index as a formula.
Element i moves to (i + k) % n. Allocate a fresh array and place each element directly at its destination.
Copy the result back into nums so the rotation is 'in-place' from the caller's view, even though we used a temp array.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to fill the temp array plus one pass to copy back → O(n) time. The temp array of size n → O(n) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
The most reliable way to *understand* the rotation is to write the destination of each element as a closed-form index, then just place elements there.

**The mapping is the entire problem.** A right rotation by `k` sends the element at index `i` to index `(i + k) mod n`. The `mod n` is what implements the wrap-around: when `i + k` runs off the end, it cycles back to the front. Element `n−1` with `k = 3`, `n = 7` goes to `(6 + 3) % 7 = 2`, which is exactly where the old last element should land after three elements wrap around. Filling a fresh array by this rule can't go wrong — there's no shifting, no overwriting order to worry about, every element is dropped directly into its final home.

**Why `k %= n` matters even here.** If `k ≥ n`, `(i + k) % n` still works mathematically, but reducing `k` first keeps the intent obvious and avoids surprises in languages where `%` on large values is awkward. It also makes the connection to the three-reversal method (which *requires* `k < n` for the split point) explicit.

**Why this isn't the final answer.** The interviewer's follow-up is almost always 'can you do it with O(1) extra space?'. The temp array is O(n) memory we'd love to avoid. But this version earns its keep: it gives you an unambiguous correctness reference to check the trickier in-place method against. State it, then say 'we can avoid the extra array with reversals.'
approaches.insight: Naming the destination formula (i + k) % n converts a vague 'shift things over' into a precise placement rule. Every correct rotation method must reproduce this mapping — it's your ground truth.

dryRun.intro: out[(i + 3) % 7] = nums[i]. Each element jumps straight to its destination.

code.python:
def rotate(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> None:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n
    out = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        out[(i + k) % n] = nums[i]
    nums[:] = out

java.explanation: Collapse rotations of full multiples of n; k can exceed n.
Place each element at its rotated destination; %n wraps around.
Copy back so the caller sees nums mutated in place.

python.explanation: Direct placement by the destination formula.
Slice assignment mutates the original list object in place.

edgeCases.behavior: Every element maps to its own index → array unchanged.

pitfalls: Using `return nums[:]` in Python or reassigning nums = out — that rebinds the local name and doesn't mutate the caller's list; use nums[:] = out.
Skipping k %= n and indexing out of range when k > n.
Claiming this is O(1) space — it isn't; be honest about the temp array.

approaches.name: Three Reversals (Optimal, O(1) Space)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for the O(1)-space follow-up. Explain WHY the reversals compose into a rotation — don't just recite the three calls.
hints: After k %= n, the answer is the last k elements followed by the first n−k elements. What does reversing the entire array do to those two blocks?
Reverse the whole array: now the last k elements are at the front but in reversed order, and the first n−k are at the back, also reversed.
Reverse the first k elements to fix their order, then reverse the remaining n−k to fix theirs. Three in-place reversals, each a two-pointer swap.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each element is touched by exactly one reversal (the whole-array reverse counts as one), so total swaps ≈ n → O(n) time. Reversal swaps in place with two indices → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
The target layout after a right rotation by `k` is: **last `k` elements, then first `n−k` elements**, each block keeping its internal order. The three-reversal trick reaches that layout using only swaps.

**Step 1 — reverse the whole array.** Take `[1,2,3,4,5,6,7]` with `k = 3`. Reversing everything gives `[7,6,5,4,3,2,1]`. Look at what happened structurally: the last `k = 3` elements `(5,6,7)` are now at the *front* — exactly where they belong — but in reversed order `(7,6,5)`. Likewise the first `n−k = 4` elements `(1,2,3,4)` are now at the *back*, reversed to `(4,3,2,1)`. So one global reverse puts both blocks in the right *region* but with their internal order flipped.

**Step 2 — reverse the first `k`.** Reversing `nums[0..k)` un-flips the front block: `[7,6,5]` → `[5,6,7]`. The array is now `[5,6,7,4,3,2,1]`. The front is finished.

**Step 3 — reverse the last `n−k`.** Reversing `nums[k..n)` un-flips the back block: `[4,3,2,1]` → `[1,2,3,4]`, giving `[5,6,7,1,2,3,4]` — the rotation, done.

**Why this composes correctly in general.** Reversal is an involution that maps position `j` within a segment to its mirror. Doing it globally then locally is algebraically equivalent to a cyclic shift: the global reverse sends index `i` to `n−1−i`; reversing the two sub-segments then sends each element to precisely `(i + k) mod n` — the same destination the index-map method computed. That equivalence is why you can trust it matches the brute-force ground truth.

**Why `k %= n` is mandatory here.** The split point for steps 2 and 3 is index `k`. If `k ≥ n`, that split is out of bounds and the reversals are nonsensical. Reducing `k` modulo `n` first guarantees `0 ≤ k < n` so the two sub-segments are well-defined (and `k = 0` becomes three no-op reverses, correctly leaving the array unchanged).
approaches.insight: Reverse-all-then-reverse-blocks is the canonical O(1)-space way to translate or rotate a sequence. The global reverse parks each block in the correct half; two local reverses repair the internal order. The same three-step move rotates strings and reorders words in a sentence.

dryRun.intro: k %= 7 = 3. Watch the array transform through three reversals.

code.python:
def rotate(self, nums: list[int], k: int) -> None:
    n = len(nums)
    k %= n

    def reverse(lo: int, hi: int) -> None:
        while lo < hi:
            nums[lo], nums[hi] = nums[hi], nums[lo]
            lo += 1
            hi -= 1

    reverse(0, n - 1)
    reverse(0, k - 1)
    reverse(k, n - 1)

java.explanation: Guarantees 0 <= k < n so the split index k is in bounds.
Whole-array reverse: both blocks land in the right half, internally flipped.
Un-flip the front block (the rotated-in suffix).
Un-flip the back block (the rotated-out prefix).

python.explanation: Reduce so the split point k is valid.
Reverse everything to relocate the two blocks.
Restore order of the first k (the new front).
Restore order of the remaining n-k.

diagrams.title: Three reversals turning into a rotation
diagrams.caption: Whole reverse, then fix each block. Highlights mark the segment being reversed.

edgeCases.behavior: k %= 2 = 1 → reverse(0,1)→[2,1], reverse(0,0) no-op, reverse(1,1) no-op → [2,1].
k becomes 0 → reverse(0,n-1) then reverse(0,-1) and reverse(0,n-1): the two full reverses cancel, leaving the array unchanged.

pitfalls: Forgetting k %= n — reverse(0, k-1) with k > n is out of bounds.
Reversing the blocks before the whole array — rotates left instead of right.
Off-by-one in the reverse bounds: it's reverse(0, k-1) and reverse(k, n-1), inclusive endpoints.

commonMistakes: Forgetting k %= n, causing TLE (rotating k times) or index-out-of-bounds.
Rotating one step at a time k times — O(n·k), far too slow for k, n up to 10⁵.
In Python, rebinding nums instead of mutating it (nums = ... vs nums[:] = ...), so the caller sees no change.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping k %= n
commonMistakesDetailed.why: k can be up to 10⁵ regardless of n. Without reduction, reverse(0, k-1) indexes past the array (Java throws) and a step-by-step rotation does k full passes (TLE).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Rebinding instead of mutating in Python
commonMistakesDetailed.why: rotate must mutate nums in place. Assigning nums = out (or returning a new list) only changes the local reference; the caller's array is untouched.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: One-step-at-a-time rotation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Popping the last element and inserting it at the front k times is O(n) per step → O(n·k). With n,k up to 1e5 that's 1e10 operations — TLE.
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
k %= len(nums)
nums[:] = nums[-k:] + nums[:-k]  # or the three-reversal method

patternNote: Reverse-all-then-reverse-blocks is the canonical O(1)-space rotation/translation of a sequence. Recognise it whenever you must cyclically shift an array or string in place. The destination identity (i + k) % n is the correctness anchor.
